source_title: Two-year effects of semaglutide in adults with overweight or obesity: the STEP 5 trial
research_question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce body weight in adults with overweight or obesity?
claim_text: In the STEP 5 trial, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg provided evidence of greater body-weight reduction than placebo at week 104 in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes.

result_summary: The paper reports an estimated mean body-weight change from baseline to week 104 of -15.2% with semaglutide versus -2.6% with placebo, with an estimated treatment difference of -12.6 percentage points.

source_title: Clinical Impact of Semaglutide in Patients with Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction
research_question: Does oral semaglutide affect cardiac biomarkers and metabolic parameters in adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a retrospective single-center cohort of 27 patients with HFpEF and T2DM, three months of oral semaglutide was associated with a significant reduction in BNP levels compared with the pre-treatment period, along with improvements in glycemic control, weight, inflammation, and cardiac structural markers.
population: Adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and type 2 diabetes mellitus who initiated oral semaglutide at a single academic center (n=27).
intervention: Oral semaglutide, initiated for type 2 diabetes management.
comparator: Within-subject pre-treatment period (same patients, three months before initiation); single-arm design, no separate control group.
outcome: Change in log-transformed B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) from pre-treatment to on-treatment period; secondary: HbA1c, body weight, C-reactive protein, left atrial volume index, left ventricular mass index.
result_summary: Log BNP was stable during the pre-treatment period (p=0.34) but decreased significantly during the on-treatment period (p<0.001); reduction during on-treatment was significantly greater than during pre-treatment (mean difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.44 to -0.11, p<0.001). Concomitant reductions were observed in HbA1c, body weight, C-reactive protein, left atrial volume index, and left ventricular mass index; CRP change correlated with BNP change (r=0.46, p=0.015).
short_source_excerpt: Log BNP remained stable during the pre-treatment period ... but decreased significantly during the on-treatment period
limitations: Single-arm pre/post design; no separate control or placebo group.
Small sample size (n=27) from a single academic center.
Short follow-up (three months on-treatment).
Observational, not randomized -- cannot rule out regression to the mean or unmeasured confounding.
uncertainty_notes: This evidence bears on the research question via a small single-center pre/post cohort; it should be weighed alongside larger and/or randomized comparisons of GLP-1-class therapy in HFpEF before drawing a corpus-level conclusion.
confidence_note: High confidence that the extracted result and PICO fields are directly reflected in the paper's abstract; not a confidence score for the underlying study's methodological strength or a corpus-level conclusion.

source_title: Effects of Semaglutide on Cardiometabolic Risk in People with Obesity, With and Without Type 2 Diabetes: A Retrospective Observational Study
research_question: Does semaglutide improve body composition and cardiometabolic risk factors in adults with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a real-world retrospective cohort of 70 adults with obesity (with and without T2DM), semaglutide treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight, waist circumference, HbA1c, blood pressure, and visceral fat, with more pronounced glycemic improvement among participants with T2DM.
population: 70 adults with obesity, 42 with type 2 diabetes and 28 without, treated with semaglutide per current clinical guidelines.
comparator: Within-subject pre-treatment baseline; single-arm observational design, no separate control group.
outcome: Body weight, waist circumference, fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c (primary); lipid profile, insulin resistance indices, inflammatory markers, hepatic parameters, body composition (secondary).
result_summary: Semaglutide was associated with reductions in body weight (-9 kg), waist circumference (-8 cm), HbA1c (-1.1%), systolic blood pressure (-7.5 mmHg), visceral fat area (-30.1 cm2), and insulin resistance markers. Glycemic improvements were more pronounced in participants with T2DM; skeletal muscle mass was relatively preserved.
short_source_excerpt: Semaglutide treatment was associated with significant reductions in body weight (-9 kg), waist circumference (-8 cm), HbA1c (-1.1%)
limitations: No control or comparator group; cannot isolate semaglutide's effect from other concurrent lifestyle changes.
Retrospective observational design.
Predictor-of-response findings (baseline HbA1c, visceral adiposity) are exploratory.
uncertainty_notes: Bears on the broader obesity/metabolic-syndrome question, but as a single uncontrolled real-world cohort it should be read alongside randomized trial evidence for semaglutide's weight and metabolic effects.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

research_question: Is oral semaglutide associated with improved heart-failure health status and weight loss in adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes, and obesity?
claim_text: In a propensity-score-matched real-world cohort of patients with HFrEF, type 2 diabetes, and obesity, oral semaglutide was associated with greater improvement in heart-failure health status and greater weight loss at 24 months than no GLP-1 receptor agonist use.
population: Adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes, and obesity (162 matched per group after 1:1 propensity-score matching; mean age 71.0, mean BMI 32.1, 52.9% female).
comparator: No glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (Control group).
outcome: Heart failure health status (>=5-point change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score) and change in body weight at 24 months.
result_summary: Oral-Sema group patients were more likely to have improved HF health status (OR 2.45, 95% CI 1.25-3.65, p=0.012). source_title: Weight-loss dynamics with tirzepatide versus semaglutide
research_question: How does weight-loss magnitude and adverse-event profile compare between tirzepatide and semaglutide in real-world use for obesity and type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched real-world cohort, tirzepatide was associated with greater and faster weight loss than semaglutide, with lower prevalence of gastrointestinal and systemic adverse events, and demographic variation in treatment response for both drugs.
population: Adults treated with tirzepatide or semaglutide for obesity/type 2 diabetes; 10,339 tirzepatide-treated and 10,339 semaglutide-treated patients after 1:1 propensity matching on age, sex, T2D status, baseline BMI/weight, index year, and follow-up duration.
outcome: Maximum weight loss over 2 years (categorized into five response groups), weight-loss velocity, adverse-event prevalence (AI-curated from clinical notes), pre-/post-treatment disease-prevalence changes.
result_summary: Tirzepatide-treated patients lost more weight than semaglutide-treated patients (mean reduction 14.7% vs 10.8%, p<0.001); high-response rate (>=15% weight loss in year 1) was nearly doubled with tirzepatide (42.6% vs 21.6%, p<0.001), with faster monthly weight-loss velocity (2.54% vs 2.18%). Tirzepatide was associated with lower prevalence of GI and systemic adverse events. Women and White patients were more represented among high responders for both drugs; Black and Hispanic patients were more represented among minimal-response patients.
short_source_excerpt: Patients treated with tirzepatide lost more weight than those treated with semaglutide (mean reduction, 14.7 vs. 10.8%; P < 0.001)
limitations: Retrospective EHR cohort, not randomized; comparative effectiveness, not a head-to-head trial.
Adverse events identified via AI-enabled curation of clinical notes -- the curation method's own accuracy is not independently validated in this record.
Demographic-subgroup response differences are exploratory and may reflect access/prescribing patterns rather than biological response differences.
uncertainty_notes: Directly relevant to the corpus's 'Dual incretin therapies such as tirzepatide' subtopic as a head-to-head comparator to GLP-1 monotherapy; should be read alongside randomized head-to-head trials where available.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Tirzepatide for Recurrent Weight Gain after Bariatric Procedures: Real-World Evidence of Efficacy and Safety
research_question: Is tirzepatide effective and safe for treating recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery or endoscopic bariatric therapy?
claim_text: In an observational cohort of patients with recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery or endoscopic bariatric therapy, 24 weeks of tirzepatide was associated with substantial total body weight loss and was generally well tolerated.
population: 34 patients (26 female, 8 male) with recurrent weight gain after bariatric surgery (n=32) or endoscopic bariatric therapy (n=2).
intervention: Once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide, dosing range 2.5-10 mg/week, for 24 weeks.
comparator: Within-subject baseline (pre-treatment); single-arm design, no separate control group.
outcome: Percentage total body weight loss (%TBWL), waist circumference, BMI category shift, adverse events, at 24 weeks.
result_summary: Mean %TBWL was 18.1 +/- 5.6% (p<0.0001), with significant waist circumference reduction (p<0.0001); most patients shifted to lower BMI categories, with the majority reaching overweight or normal weight status. Adverse events were exclusively gastrointestinal (constipation, diarrhea, nausea), generally mild, with no treatment discontinuations.
short_source_excerpt: the mean percentage total body weight loss (%TBWL) was 18.1 +/- 5.6% (p < 0.0001)
limitations: Small sample size (n=34).
Single-arm design, no comparator group.
Short follow-up (24 weeks).
Authors themselves describe the evidence as 'preliminary'.
uncertainty_notes: A narrow but clinically specific slice of tirzepatide evidence (post-bariatric weight regain) rather than general obesity treatment; should not be generalized to first-line obesity treatment without further evidence.

source_title: Shifts in waist-to-height ratio categories within tirzepatide groups: a post-hoc analysis of SURMOUNT-1
research_question: Does tirzepatide improve waist-to-height ratio category in adults with obesity or overweight, relative to placebo?
claim_text: In a post-hoc analysis of the SURMOUNT-1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, tirzepatide was associated with sustained improvement in waist-to-height ratio category compared with placebo, in adults with obesity or overweight.
population: 2,538 SURMOUNT-1 participants with obesity or overweight (BMI >=30 or >=27 kg/m2 with at least one obesity-related complication, excluding diabetes), with or without prediabetes.
intervention: Once-weekly tirzepatide (5, 10, or 15 mg) plus reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
comparator: Placebo plus the same reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
outcome: Shift in waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) category (<=0.49, >0.49 to <=0.59, >0.59, per NICE framework) from baseline to week 72, and week 176 in the prediabetes subgroup.
result_summary: At baseline, 89.8% of participants had WHtR >0.59. After 72 weeks of tirzepatide (10/15 mg), 16.7% achieved WHtR <=0.49 and 54.7% improved their baseline category, versus 9.6% with placebo. At 176 weeks, among participants with prediabetes, 12.2% achieved WHtR <=0.49 and 46.4% improved category with tirzepatide versus 9.3% with placebo.
short_source_excerpt: After 72 weeks of tirzepatide (10/15 mg), 16.7% of participants achieved a WHtR <= 0.49, and 54.7% improved their baseline WHtR category compared to 9.6% with placebo
limitations: Post-hoc analysis, not a pre-specified primary endpoint of SURMOUNT-1.
WHtR is a surrogate anthropometric marker, not a direct clinical cardiometabolic outcome.
Excludes participants with diabetes at baseline.
uncertainty_notes: Randomized, placebo-controlled source trial gives this record stronger internal validity than the other tirzepatide records in this batch, but the WHtR endpoint itself is a post-hoc, surrogate measure.

source_title: Comparative effectiveness of tirzepatide and DPP-4 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes with heart failure
research_question: How does tirzepatide compare with DPP-4 inhibitors on mortality, hospitalization, and cardiovascular outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure?
claim_text: In a propensity-matched real-world cohort of patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure, tirzepatide was associated with markedly lower hazards of mortality, hospitalization, heart-failure exacerbation, and major adverse cardiovascular events than DPP-4 inhibitors.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure treated between 2022 and 2025 (8,956 matched pairs after propensity-score matching); prespecified subgroups for HFrEF and HFnonrEF.
outcome: All-cause mortality, hospitalization, heart-failure exacerbation, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
result_summary: Tirzepatide was associated with a lower hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.25-0.42), hospitalizations (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.48-0.57), HF exacerbation (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.33-0.42), and MACE (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73-0.84). Subgroup analyses for HFrEF and HFnonrEF showed similar trends.
short_source_excerpt: treatment with tirzepatide was associated with markedly lower hazards of mortality, hospitalization, HF exacerbation, and MACE compared to DPP-4 inhibitors
limitations: Retrospective, non-randomized comparative-effectiveness design; residual confounding by indication possible despite propensity matching.
Active comparator is DPP-4 inhibitors, not placebo.
uncertainty_notes: A large, comparative real-world signal for tirzepatide in a cardiac-comorbid T2DM population; the very large effect sizes (e.g. HR 0.32 for mortality) warrant caution and comparison against randomized evidence where available.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Comparing measured and reported change in gastrointestinal symptoms after initiation of metformin treatment: a questionnaire validation study
research_question: Do self-reported and directly measured changes in gastrointestinal symptoms agree after initiation of metformin treatment for type 2 diabetes in primary care?
claim_text: In a Swedish primary-care cohort initiating metformin for type 2 diabetes, a newly constructed gastrointestinal-symptom questionnaire showed moderate-to-good agreement between measured and self-reported symptom change for most of six assessed symptoms.
population: 54 participants with type 2 diabetes in Swedish primary care (the MEMO study -- Interaction Between Metformin and Microbiota), assessed at baseline and after 2 months of metformin treatment.
intervention: Metformin treatment, with GI-symptom assessment via questionnaire at baseline and 2 months.
comparator: Within-subject before/after comparison; this is a measurement-validation study, not a controlled treatment-effect study.
outcome: Agreement (Spearman's rho) between measured change (difference between two timepoint assessments) and directly reported/perceived change in six gastrointestinal symptoms.
result_summary: Spearman's rho exceeded 0.4 for 4 of 6 symptoms: poor appetite 0.60 (95% CI 0.39-0.75), loose stool/diarrhea 0.58 (95% CI 0.37-0.74), flatulence 0.45 (95% CI 0.21-0.64), abdominal pain 0.45 (95% CI 0.20-0.65). Agreement was lower for nausea and vomiting, though numerically above 75% agreement, likely due to few symptomatic participants overall.
short_source_excerpt: The agreement between reported and measured change of symptoms, measured as Spearman's rho, was above 0.4 for 4 out of 6 symptoms
limitations: This study validates a measurement questionnaire; it does not itself estimate metformin's GI-symptom incidence, severity, or causal effect.
Small sample (n=54), single-country primary-care setting.
No comparator arm without metformin -- cannot separate metformin-attributable symptom change from other causes.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' rather than 'supports'/'contradicts' because this record is about the reliability of a measurement instrument for tracking metformin's known GI side-effect profile, not a direct claim about whether metformin causes or how often it causes GI symptoms. Useful context for interpreting other metformin-tolerability evidence in this corpus, including the imeglimin-replacement record in this same batch.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's methodological strength.

source_title: Imeglimin as a Replacement Therapy for Metformin in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Experiencing Metformin Intolerance: A Retrospective Observational Study
research_question: Is imeglimin an effective and tolerable alternative to metformin in adults with type 2 diabetes who have metformin intolerance?
claim_text: In a retrospective cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes and documented metformin intolerance, switching to imeglimin was associated with meaningful improvements in glycemic control and a favorable safety and tolerability profile over three months.
population: 100 adults with type 2 diabetes and documented metformin intolerance, initiated on imeglimin monotherapy or combination therapy for three months.
intervention: Imeglimin (monotherapy or combination therapy), replacing metformin.
comparator: Within-subject baseline (pre-switch) versus 3-month follow-up; no active metformin comparator arm, since the cohort is defined by metformin intolerance.
outcome: HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), postprandial plasma glucose (PPG) (primary); body weight, lipid profile, renal function, gastrointestinal side-effect rate (secondary).
result_summary: HbA1c decreased from 7.96 +/- 1.56% to 7.35 +/- 1.02% (mean change -0.62 +/- 1.05%, p<0.001, n=77); FPG decreased by 32.18 mg/dL and PPG by 44.63 mg/dL (both p<0.001). Body weight decreased modestly (-0.81 kg, p<0.001); LDL cholesterol and triglycerides decreased significantly; eGFR remained stable (p=0.135); GI side effects occurred in only 2% of patients.
short_source_excerpt: Imeglimin demonstrated meaningful improvements in glycemic control, with a favorable safety and tolerability profile in metformin-intolerant patients
limitations: Retrospective, single-arm design; by definition the cohort cannot include a concurrent metformin-tolerant comparator arm.
Short follow-up (3 months).
Single-country/setting; generalizability not established.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'contextualizes' rather than 'supports'/'contradicts' because this record is not a direct claim about metformin's own effect -- it is evidence about managing metformin's well-known GI-intolerance limitation, directly relevant to the corpus's 'Metformin and type 2 diabetes treatment' subtopic as a limitations/alternatives data point.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes
research_question: Are SGLT2 inhibitors associated with renal and cardiovascular benefit, and what safety trade-offs, in elderly adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a propensity-matched retrospective cohort of elderly adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with significant renoprotective effects, particularly among those with preserved baseline renal function, alongside an increased risk of genital infections.
population: Diabetic patients aged >=65 years who received antihyperglycemic therapy at a single Taiwan hospital, 2021-2023 (9,915 total; SGLT2i users n=3,345, non-users n=6,570; 1,529 matched pairs after 1:1 propensity-score matching).
outcome: Renal function (30%/50% eGFR decline), coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, heart failure (primary); urinary tract infection, genital infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, hypoglycemia (secondary); MACE occurrence and recurrence.
result_summary: SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced risk of 30% eGFR decline (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59-0.80, p<0.001) and 50% eGFR decline (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.45-0.80, p<0.001), with greater benefit at higher baseline eGFR (>=50 mL/min/1.73 m2). Genital infection risk was increased (HR 4.29, 95% CI 1.02-18.04, p=0.047) in patients without prior history of such infections. First MACE occurrence did not differ significantly (log-rank p=0.160), but MACE recurrence was markedly reduced (log-rank p<0.001).
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with significant renoprotective effects, demonstrated by reduced risk of 30% eGFR decline (HR 0.69
limitations: Single-center, retrospective design.
Observational propensity-score matching cannot fully rule out unmeasured confounding.
Genital-infection finding is based on a subgroup without prior infection history and a wide confidence interval (1.02-18.04).
uncertainty_notes: Direction is marked 'supports' for the primary renoprotective finding, but the record's own limitations/result_summary preserve the genital-infection safety trade-off -- read both together, not the direction alone.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: SGLT2 inhibitor use and disparities in all-cause mortality in type 2 diabetes: insights from a multi-ethnic population
research_question: Does the mortality benefit of SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) use in adults with type 2 diabetes differ by ethnicity, including Indigenous populations?
claim_text: In a New Zealand multi-ethnic primary-care population with type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin use was associated with lower all-cause mortality across ethnic groups, with the largest relative benefit observed in Maori and Pacific people.
population: Adults aged 18-75 with type 2 diabetes in the Auckland/Waikato regions of New Zealand, February 2021-December 2023 (n=59,505 primary-care records, linked to national medication-dispensing and mortality records 2021-2024); 12,792 matched pairs after propensity matching.
intervention: Empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor), with funded, prioritized access for Maori and Pacific people.
outcome: All-cause mortality, stratified by ethnicity and by cardiovascular/renal disease/risk (CVRD) status.
result_summary: Annualized crude mortality was higher in those not dispensed SGLT2i than in those receiving it (35.2 vs 13.1 per 1000/year with CVRD; 7.7 vs 3.6 without CVRD). After adjustment, the greatest mortality difference with SGLT2i use was in Maori (HR 0.475, 95% CI 0.336-0.672, p<0.001), followed by Pacific people (HR 0.507, 95% CI 0.395-0.651, p<0.001) and European people (HR 0.667, 95% CI 0.545-0.816, p<0.001).
short_source_excerpt: the greatest difference in mortality with SGLT2i use was seen in Maori (HR 0.475
limitations: Observational, linked-records design; residual confounding and differential ascertainment across ethnic groups are possible.
Single country/health system, and specific to empagliflozin rather than the SGLT2-inhibitor class generally.
uncertainty_notes: Adds an equity-relevant finding within the SGLT2-inhibitor subtopic: the direction of benefit is consistent across groups, but the magnitude varies meaningfully by ethnicity -- worth preserving as a distinct nuance, not collapsing into a single pooled effect size.

source_title: Safety of SGLT2 inhibitors versus DPP-4 inhibitors in super-elderly patients (>= 80 years) with type 2 diabetes: a propensity score-matched cohort study
research_question: How does the safety profile of SGLT2 inhibitors compare with DPP-4 inhibitors in super-elderly (>=80 years) adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched cohort of super-elderly adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors showed a favorable safety profile relative to DPP-4 inhibitors on most outcomes, including lower falls, fracture, and mortality risk, but higher genital candidiasis and heart-failure hospitalization risk.
population: Adults aged >=80 years with type 2 diabetes newly prescribed SGLT2i or DPP-4i, from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (176 healthcare organizations); 65,119 matched pairs after propensity-score matching (mean age 82.2, 48.7% female).
outcome: Falls, hip fracture, acute kidney injury, urinary tract infection, genital candidiasis, hypoglycemia, volume depletion, hypotension, syncope (primary); stroke, myocardial infarction, heart-failure hospitalization, all-cause mortality (secondary).
result_summary: Over a mean follow-up of 269 days, SGLT2i was associated with lower risk of falls (HR 0.90), hip fracture (HR 0.78), acute kidney injury (HR 0.82), urinary tract infection (HR 0.79), hypoglycemia (HR 0.74), volume depletion (HR 0.91), stroke (HR 0.88), and all-cause mortality (HR 0.73; all p<0.05). Genital candidiasis risk was higher with SGLT2i (HR 1.70, p<0.001), as was heart-failure hospitalization (HR 1.07, p=0.007). Hypotension, syncope, and myocardial infarction did not differ significantly.
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2i demonstrated a favorable safety profile compared to DPP-4i, with significantly lower risks of falls (10%), hip fracture (22%) ... Safety concerns included increased genital candidiasis (70%) and modestly higher heart failure hospitalization (7%)
limitations: Retrospective active-comparator design; residual confounding possible despite propensity matching.
Short mean follow-up (269 days).
TriNetX multi-site network introduces site-level heterogeneity.
Super-elderly patients are historically underrepresented in randomized trials, so this fills a real evidence gap but remains non-randomized.
uncertainty_notes: Marked 'qualifies' rather than 'supports' because the safety picture is genuinely two-sided: favorable on most outcomes, unfavorable on two (genital candidiasis, heart-failure hospitalization) -- both directions are preserved in result_summary and should not be collapsed into a single favorable/unfavorable label.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Comparative effects of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists on osteoarthritis risk in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A multi-institutional cohort study
research_question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists compare on osteoarthritis risk in adults with type 2 diabetes?
claim_text: In a large propensity-matched cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with a lower risk of osteoarthritis, particularly knee osteoarthritis, compared with GLP-1 receptor agonist use.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes newly prescribed either SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists between January 2017 and December 2019, from the TriNetX database; 452,445 matched pairs after propensity-score matching.
outcome: Osteoarthritis (OA) incidence over five years (primary); knee OA, hip OA, total knee arthroplasty, total hip arthroplasty, major joint injections (secondary).
result_summary: The SGLT2-inhibitor group had a significantly lower risk of OA compared with the GLP-1-RA group (HR 0.921, 95% CI 0.895-0.946), with a greater reduction for knee OA specifically (HR 0.831, 95% CI 0.783-0.882). No significant differences were observed in total hip or knee arthroplasty risk. SGLT2-inhibitor users also had fewer major joint injections (HR 0.915, 95% CI 0.882-0.951).

limitations: Retrospective comparative-effectiveness design; channeling bias is plausible if patients selected for one drug class differ systematically in baseline OA risk or mobility.
Association study; no mechanistic validation of a causal pathway.
Residual confounding possible despite very large-scale propensity matching.

source_title: Comparative Effects of SGLT2 Inhibitors and GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Composite Surrogate Markers of Insulin Resistance: A Real-World Study Using METS-IR and SPISE
research_question: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists compare in their effects on composite surrogate markers of insulin resistance in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity?
claim_text: In a real-world cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, both GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors significantly improved composite surrogate markers of insulin resistance over six months, with no significant difference between the two drug classes.
population: 100 individuals with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, treated with either GLP-1RA (n=54) or SGLT2i (n=46) with stable concomitant pharmacotherapy, followed for 6 months.
intervention: GLP-1 receptor agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor.
comparator: The two drug classes compared head-to-head; no placebo arm.
outcome: Change in METS-IR (Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance) and SPISE (Single Point Insulin Sensitivity Estimator), alongside BMI and HbA1c.
result_summary: Both groups showed significant improvement in METS-IR (GLP-1RA -3.9 +/- 5.9; SGLT2i -2.5 +/- 2.6; both p<0.001) and SPISE (GLP-1RA +0.46 +/- 0.52; SGLT2i +0.44 +/- 0.61; both p<0.001), with no significant between-group difference. In the GLP-1RA group, METS-IR change correlated with BMI change (r=0.48, p<0.001) and HbA1c change (r=0.29, p=0.030); no significant correlations were observed in the SGLT2i group. Stratified analyses showed greater METS-IR reduction among individuals with BMI >=30 treated with GLP-1RA.
short_source_excerpt: Both treatment groups demonstrated significant improvements in METS-IR ... and SPISE ... with no significant between-group differences
limitations: Small sample (100 total, unevenly split between drug classes).
Observational, non-randomized comparative design.
METS-IR and SPISE are surrogate composite indices, not gold-standard insulin-sensitivity measures such as clamp studies.
Six-month follow-up only.
uncertainty_notes: Both drug classes improved the surrogate markers with no clear superiority at the group level; the BMI-stratified and correlation findings are exploratory and should not be treated as confirmed subgroup effects.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength.

source_title: Precision Prescribing of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Individuals With Type 2 Diabetes for Primary Prevention of Heart Failure: Model Development and Validation Study
research_question: Can individual-level heart-failure risk reduction from SGLT2 inhibitors be predicted for adults with type 2 diabetes who do not yet have established cardiovascular, renal, or heart-failure disease?
claim_text: A prediction model combining validated heart-failure risk estimation with trial-derived SGLT2-inhibitor relative-risk reduction was developed and validated in a large UK primary-care cohort, and SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with a lower risk of new-onset heart failure in adults with type 2 diabetes without established cardiovascular, renal, or heart-failure disease.
population: Adults with type 2 diabetes without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease; UK primary-care validation cohort with linked hospital and death records, 2013-2020 (57,368 SGLT2i initiators, 111,673 DPP-4-inhibitor/sulfonylurea comparator initiators).
intervention: SGLT2 inhibitor; model development used the SGLT2-inhibitor Absolute Benefit REsponse (SABRE) model, combining the QDiabetes-HF absolute-risk model with a trial-meta-analysis SGLT2i hazard ratio for HF hospitalization (HR 0.63).
outcome: New-onset heart failure (observed); predicted versus observed 5-year absolute heart-failure benefit (model calibration).
result_summary: SGLT2i use was associated with a 30% lower risk of new-onset heart failure (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.63-0.78), consistent with trial evidence; relative HF benefit did not vary by baseline absolute HF risk (p=0.82). The SABRE model's predicted 5-year absolute HF benefit ranged from <0.1% to 14.1% (median 1.0%, IQR 0.6-1.8%) and calibrated well against observed HF outcomes, providing more targeted HF-prevention guidance than current guidelines for this population.
short_source_excerpt: SGLT2i use was associated with a 30% lower risk of new-onset HF (HR 0.70 [95% CI 0.63-0.78]), consistent with trial evidence
limitations: The prediction model itself was built and validated on UK observational primary-care data (2013-2020), not tested in a randomized trial of the tool.
Relies on a fixed trial-meta-analysis relative-risk estimate (HR 0.63) rather than a population-specific relative-risk estimate.
Several authors disclose industry relationships (consulting/speaker fees, research funding) with SGLT2-inhibitor manufacturers, disclosed in the paper.
uncertainty_notes: Extends the corpus's SGLT2-inhibitor evidence into primary prevention (patients without yet-established ASCVD/HF/CKD), directly relevant to 'treatment response' and 'durability'/targeting questions in scientific_question.md, not just treatment effect in already-diagnosed populations.
confidence_note: High confidence the extracted fields match the abstract; not a confidence score for the study's causal strength or the prediction model's clinical readiness.
